summary: This proposed standard describes two methods for encapsulating network interconnect traffic, such as IP, over ATM Adaptation Layer 5. It was replaced by RFC 2684.

plainLanguage.summary: ATM networks send small fixed-size cells. This paper explains two ways to pack Internet messages into those cells.

questions: what is llc encapsulation over atm
how is ip carried over atm aal5
subtitle: Two ways to wrap routed and bridged network traffic inside ATM AAL5 frames.

tldr.problem: ATM carries data in short fixed-length cells, but routers and bridges need to send variable-length packets of many different protocols over it.
tldr.mechanism: The packets ride in the payload of an AAL5 CPCS-PDU, and the receiver learns the protocol either from an LLC/SNAP header (LLC Encapsulation) or from which virtual circuit the frame arrived on (VC Based Multiplexing).
tldr.outcome: This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 2684, so it is a historical definition of the method.

today: RFC 1483 was obsoleted by RFC 2684, which is now the place to look for this encapsulation. It was published in July 1993 as a Proposed Standard.

sections.title: Two Ways to Carry Network Traffic over ATM
sections.content:
This memo describes how to carry connectionless network interconnect traffic, both routed and bridged Protocol Data Units (PDUs), over an Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) network. ATM chops variable-length data into short, fixed-length cells, but this memo does not define a new segmentation method. The PDUs simply travel in the payload of the Common Part Convergence Sublayer (CPCS) PDU of ATM Adaptation Layer 5 (AAL5).

Two methods are defined. LLC Encapsulation multiplexes many protocols over one ATM virtual circuit (VC) by prefixing each PDU with an IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC) header. VC Based Multiplexing carries each protocol on its own VC, so the VC itself identifies the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to label parcels. Either stick a label on every parcel, or use a separate delivery truck for each kind of parcel.

sections.title: Choosing a Multiplexing Method
sections.content:
The RFC expects VC Based Multiplexing to dominate where creating many ATM VCs on demand is fast and cheap, most likely first in private ATM networks. LLC Encapsulation suits cases where a separate VC per protocol is impractical, for example when the network only supports (semi) Permanent Virtual Circuits, or when charging depends heavily on the number of simultaneous VCs.

The method is chosen by manual configuration for PVCs, or by B-ISDN signalling for Switched VCs. The RFC says the signalling details were still under study and leaves negotiation and address resolution for further RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: If trucks are cheap you can use one per kind of parcel. If trucks cost a lot, you put everything in one truck and label each parcel.

sections.title: The AAL5 Frame
sections.content:
Whichever method is used, the PDU goes into the Payload field of an AAL5 CPCS-PDU. The payload can be up to 2^16 - 1 octets. After it come a PAD of 0 to 47 octets, then a trailer made of CPCS-UU (1 octet), CPI (1 octet), Length (2 octets) and CRC (4 octets).

The pad makes the trailer land right-justified in the last 48-octet cell payload. CPCS-UU has no function here and can be any value. CPI only aligns the trailer to 64 bits and is coded 0x00. A Length of 0x00 means the frame is aborted. The CRC protects the whole CPCS-PDU except itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Every frame is a parcel with padding to fill the last box and a small slip at the end that says how long the parcel was and lets the receiver check nothing got broken.

sections.title: LLC Encapsulation for Routed and Bridged PDUs
sections.content:
For routed PDUs the Control field of the LLC header is always 0x03 (Unnumbered Information). The LLC value 0xFE-FE-03 means a routed ISO PDU follows, identified by its NLPID. A NLPID of 0x00 is invalid under ATM encapsulation. All other routed protocols, including IP, use the LLC value 0xAA-AA-03, which announces a SNAP header: a 3-octet OUI and a 2-octet PID. With OUI 0x00-00-00 the PID is an EtherType, which is 0x08-00 for IP. The RFC says the NLPID form must not be used for IP.

Bridged PDUs also use 0xAA-AA-03, with the 802.1 OUI 0x00-80-C2. The two-octet PID gives the media type (802.3/Ethernet, 802.4, 802.5, FDDI, 802.6 or BPDUs) and whether the original LAN FCS is kept. Padding after the PID aligns the bridged frame on a four-octet boundary.

The IP encapsulation is compatible with RFC 1042.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parcel gets a label saying what is inside. For Internet parcels the label says 'this is IP'. For bridged parcels it says which kind of local network the parcel came from.

sections.title: VC Based Multiplexing and Bridging
sections.content:
With VC Based Multiplexing, the carried protocol is identified implicitly by the VC, so no multiplexing information goes in the payload. Routed PDUs are carried as they are. Bridged PDUs use the section 4 formats with only the fields after the PID. This gives minimal bandwidth and processing overhead.

Since the PID is absent, whether a LAN FCS is present is also fixed by the VC, so PDUs with and without FCS count as different protocols.

An ATM interface acting as a bridge must be able to flood, forward and filter. Flooding sends the PDU through each relevant VC, by copying or by a multicast VC. To learn addresses dynamically, a bridged PDU must conform to the section 4 encapsulation so the receiver can associate a foreign MAC address with an ATM station.
sections.plainLanguage: When each kind of parcel has its own truck, no label is needed: you know what is inside from the truck it came on.

sections.title: Security and Open Issues
sections.content: The RFC states that security issues are not addressed in this memo. It also lists items for further study: negotiation of the multiplexing method and address resolution, left open because ATM multicasting, addressing and signalling were not yet fully standardized.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not say anything about keeping messages secret. A few details, like how two ends agree on a method, were left for later.
